blocks: two-dimensional convex polygons. Polygons are defined in OpenGL by their 3D vertices, and are mapped to two-dimensional polygons with the use of transformation and perspective projections. The OpenGL framework can be used to define specific properties at each vertex such as texture, color, and surface orientation. It is the job of the graphics card to interpolate these properties across each polygon. OpenGL does the work of defining and applying the viewport transformations that map the 3D world to a 2D screen by eliminating hidden or overlapping polygons, applying translate, rotate, and scale transformations to vertices, and managing texturing, and lighting operations.

Visual appeal and contrast have been added to the rendering by implementing lighting and perspective calculation. Three controllable lights have been placed around the origin in SimulationView so as to illuminate the scene and crate shadows. Lighting helps to create contrast and bring out the 3D shape of the interface.¹⁵ In order to shade the model, surface normals must be provided for each vertex. The amount of light (and thus the brightness) of each vertex is related to the angle between the surface normal and the vector at which the light source hits the pixel. OpenGL has a smooth shading mode which interpolates the value of the normal at each vertex to each pixel when it is rendered, and thus presented produces a very realistic looking lighting effect. In order to create a realistic looking lighting for models, the surface normal vector at each vertex should be a weighted average by surface area of normals of all the polygons which contain the vertex. That is, if a small polygon and a large polygon share a vertex, the surface normal at the vertex should be mostly determined by the larger polygon. This refinement in the vertex normals is applied by the viewer program, which calculates normals from the polygon and vertex data supplied in the input file.

SimulationView is optimized for visualization. Whereas most commercial graphical analysis packages use interpreted languages that often translate programs inefficiently into system calls, SimulationView has been written directly in C/C++ to make the OpenGL calls and interact directly with the graphics card. The result is impressive performance – SimulationView is small enough to fit on a floppy disk, yet multiple models can be loaded at once and rendered fluidly in real-time using the keyboard and mouse to interact with the model.
The most unique feature of SimulationView, when compared with commercial graphics packages, is that it allows multiple frames of a simulation to be viewed in

sequence, producing an animation. The ability to view sequential frames gives the user a very visual idea of where, when, and how quickly structures form and grow. Without the ability to view time evolution, one would have to draw each frame separately and attempt to infer information about when and at what rate growth events took place. The model can be manipulated and rotated as it evolves, effectively providing four dimensions for exploration. The camera can be pointed, for instance, at a particular point or feature of interest in the model, and that feature can then be moved forward and backward through time.

Although SimulationView was written specifically for viewing 3D phase-field simulation results, it was easily adapted to dramatically improve the modeling of three-dimensional dendrite reconstructions. 3D dendrite reconstructions are performed by coarsening a two-phase sample (Sn-Pb is commonly used), and using a high-precision milling machine to mill off micron-thin layers of material. After a layer of material is removed by the milling machine, a digital picture of the microstructure is taken through a microscope and the process is repeated. The pictures that are generated can then be “stacked” on top of each other with a computer to reconstruct the dendrite model.

Unfortunately, the detail involved in 3D reconstruction can produce models with upwards of 2 million polygons. Today’s fastest commercial graphics cards are designed to render on the order of 100,000 polygons per second fluidly, so the size of the dendrite model surpasses the rendering capabilities of the graphics card by about an order of magnitude. Thus large dendrite files are extremely slow to load, and manipulation of the dendrites is choppy and sluggish. Polygon simplification algorithms developed by Michael Garland were used to reduce the number of polygons used to represent the reconstructions.¹⁶ The results of simplification are shown in Figure 8.

An effect of performing polygon simplification was a dramatic decrease in the size of the dendrite reconstruction files. The files can now be put on a disk or sent via email and rendered with SimulationView. Additionally, Gaussian and mean curvature calculations, which took on the order of a day for large reconstructions, can be performed virtually instantaneously in SimulationView using curvature approximation algorithms developed by Fialkowski, Aksimentiev, and Holyst.¹⁷ Mean and Gaussian curvatures are two important parameters which are used to characterize dendritic systems.
